question: How do the Panama Canal and the Suez Canal differ in the way they were built and in how a ship actually gets through each one?
answer: The Suez Canal (opened 17 November 1869, about 193 km, linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, built by Ferdinand de Lesseps' Suez Canal Company) is a sea-level canal: it has no locks at all, seawater flows freely along it, and a ship simply sails from one end to the other, usually in a convoy. The Panama Canal (opened in 1914, about 82 km, linking the Atlantic and the Pacific across the Isthmus of Panama) is a lock canal: flights of locks lift each ship about 26 m up to the artificial Gatun Lake, it crosses the lake and the Culebra Cut, and a second set of locks lowers it back to sea level on the other coast, a passage of roughly 8 to 12 hours. The United States built Panama's canal and ran it until the handover to Panama on 31 December 1999 under the 1977 Torrijos-Carter Treaties; a third, larger set of locks for 'Neopanamax' ships opened in June 2016. Egypt nationalised Suez in 1956 and added a parallel channel along part of the route in the 2010s. So the short version: Suez is longer, older and flat; Panama is shorter, younger and climbs over a lake using locks.
rubric: Suez: sea-level canal, no locks; Mediterranean to Red Sea; opened 1869; about 193 km
Panama: lock canal; ships are raised about 26 m to Gatun Lake and lowered again; Atlantic to Pacific; opened 1914; about 82 km
Governance detail is a plus: US built and controlled Panama's canal until the 31 December 1999 handover; 2016 expansion locks; Suez nationalised 1956
Penalize: claiming Suez has locks or Panama is a sea-level canal
Penalize: putting the Panama Canal before the Suez Canal in time, or swapping the oceans/seas each connects

question: Compare dromedaries with Bactrian camels: hump count, native regions, and which is more numerous.
answer: The dromedary has one hump and is native to West Asia, North Africa, the Sahara and South Asia; the Bactrian camel has two humps and comes from Central Asia (the historical region of Bactria, roughly today's Afghanistan and neighbours, plus Mongolia and western China). The dromedary is far more common: about 94% of the world's camels, against about 6% for the Bactrian. Both humps are reservoirs of fatty tissue, not water tanks; the water-in-the-hump idea is a myth. The Bactrian's thick coat suits cold, high steppe and desert winters, while the dromedary is built for hot deserts and can go about 10 days between drinks even in heat. A separate wild Bactrian species still survives in the Gobi, critically endangered with roughly 1,000 animals, and is not the ancestor of the domestic Bactrian. Oddly, the largest free-living dromedary population is in Australia, where more than a million feral animals descend from camels imported for transport in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

Plus: wild Bactrian is a distinct endangered species (~1,000); over a million feral dromedaries in Australia
Penalize: swapping the hump counts, or saying the hump stores water

question: I'm flying from Mexico City to Cusco next week. Were the Aztecs and the Incas around at the same time, and how did each empire end?
answer: Yes, they overlapped almost exactly, though they never knew of each other. The Aztec Empire was the Triple Alliance formed in 1428 around Tenochtitlan (founded 1325 on an island in the Valley of Mexico, under today's Mexico City) and ruled much of central Mexico; its language was Nahuatl and it kept pictorial codices. The Inca Empire began its expansion from Cusco around 1438 and became the largest state in pre-Columbian America, running along the Andes from Ecuador through Peru and Bolivia into Chile and Argentina; its language was Quechua and it kept records on knotted-string quipus rather than writing. Both fell to small Spanish forces within twelve years of each other. Hernan Cortes, with Indigenous allies such as Tlaxcala and helped by a smallpox epidemic, took Tenochtitlan on 13 August 1521 and captured its last ruler, Cuauhtemoc. Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532, had him executed on 29 August 1533, and took Cusco; a rump Inca state held out at Vilcabamba until 1572. So the Aztecs lasted roughly 1428 to 1521, the Incas roughly 1438 to 1533.
rubric: Both empires existed at the same time: Aztec Triple Alliance from 1428 (Tenochtitlan, central Mexico); Inca expansion from about 1438 (Cusco, Andes)
Aztec end: Hernan Cortes takes Tenochtitlan, 13 August 1521 (Cuauhtemoc last ruler); smallpox and Indigenous allies as factors
Inca end: Francisco Pizarro captures Atahualpa (1532) and executes him (29 August 1533); Vilcabamba resistance to 1572
Plus: Nahuatl vs Quechua; codices vs quipu; Inca was the larger empire
Penalize: assigning Cortes to the Incas or Pizarro to the Aztecs
Penalize: saying the two empires were centuries apart or that one conquered the other

question: What is the Lightning Network, and why do people say it lets Bitcoin handle small, fast payments?
answer: The Lightning Network is a second-layer payment protocol that runs on top of Bitcoin rather than a separate blockchain or coin. It was proposed by Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja in a white paper published in February 2015, and implementations such as Lightning Labs' went live on mainnet in 2018. Two parties open a payment channel by locking bitcoin in a funding transaction on the blockchain; after that they can exchange as many signed balance updates as they like off-chain, instantly and for negligible fees, and only the final state is written to the blockchain when the channel closes. You do not need a direct channel with everyone: payments are routed across a chain of channels through intermediate nodes, secured with hash time-locked contracts so that each hop either completes or refunds, and wrapped in onion routing so each node only learns the next hop. That is why it suits coffee-sized payments the base chain cannot do cheaply. The trade-offs: opening and closing still cost on-chain transactions; a route needs enough liquidity in each channel for the amount, so large payments can fail; channel partners must watch for a counterparty broadcasting an old state (or delegate that to a watchtower); and funds in a channel are hot funds. As of early 2026 the public network had on the order of 17,000 nodes and 40,000 channels.
rubric: Second layer on Bitcoin, not a separate blockchain or token; Poon and Dryja white paper (2015), live from 2018
Payment channels: on-chain funding transaction to open, off-chain signed balance updates, on-chain close settles the final state
Routing through intermediate nodes using hash time-locked contracts (HTLCs) and onion routing
Limitations: on-chain cost to open/close, channel liquidity limits payment size, need to be online or use watchtowers
Penalize: describing Lightning as its own blockchain, sidechain or altcoin, or saying every Lightning payment is recorded on the Bitcoin blockchain

question: Explain why Bitcoin blocks keep arriving about every ten minutes even though the amount of mining power changes all the time.
answer: Because the protocol retunes the puzzle. Mining is a lottery: a miner wins a block by finding a header hash below a target number, and the lower the target, the harder it is. Every 2016 blocks, which at ten minutes each is exactly two weeks, every node looks at the timestamps and compares how long those 2016 blocks actually took with the expected two weeks; the new target is the old target scaled by actual time divided by two weeks. If more hashing power joined and blocks came too fast, the target shrinks and difficulty rises; if miners left and blocks were slow, difficulty falls. The measured timespan is clamped to between a quarter and four times two weeks, so difficulty can move at most by a factor of four in one step. Difficulty itself is just the ratio difficulty_1_target / current_target. Nothing central sets it: each node computes the same number from the same chain. Two caveats: inside a two-week period the rate does drift (a sudden hash-rate crash means slow blocks until the next retarget), and block arrival is random, so ten minutes is only an average; individual gaps of a minute or an hour are normal.
rubric: Blocks need a hash below a target; difficulty is adjusted (retargeted) every 2016 blocks, about two weeks
The adjustment is proportional: actual time for the last 2016 blocks compared with two weeks; faster blocks mean higher difficulty and vice versa
Plus: each step is capped at a factor of 4 up or down; computed by every node from timestamps, no central authority; difficulty = difficulty_1_target / current_target
Mentions that 10 minutes is an average and that within a period the rate can drift
Penalize: saying difficulty adjusts every block, daily, or is set by miners, developers or a foundation
Penalize: saying the 10-minute spacing is enforced by a timer or by validators rejecting early blocks

question: I'm swimming at an ocean beach and suddenly I'm being dragged away from the sand and can't make any headway back. What do I do?
answer: You are almost certainly in a rip current, a narrow channel of water flowing out through the surf. First, stay calm: a rip will not drag you underwater, it only carries you away from the beach, and it weakens past the breaking waves. Do not try to swim straight back against it; rips can run at up to about 8 feet per second, faster than an Olympic swimmer, and that is how people exhaust themselves and drown. Instead swim sideways, parallel to the shoreline, until you feel the pull stop, then angle back to the beach with the breaking waves pushing you in. If you cannot escape, float or tread water, conserve energy and wave an arm and shout for help; rips often stop just beyond the surf zone and you can rest there. If you are the one on the beach watching someone else: do not swim out after them, because would-be rescuers are often the ones who die; throw something that floats, shout the parallel-swim instruction, and get a lifeguard or call the emergency number. Afterwards, prefer lifeguarded beaches and check the local surf and rip forecast; in the United States rips kill around 100 people a year and lifeguards rescue tens of thousands.
rubric: Identifies a rip current; stay calm, it pulls you out, not under
Do not swim straight back against the current (exhaustion); swim parallel to the shore until out of it, then back at an angle with the waves
If you cannot escape: float or tread water, signal and shout for help; the rip weakens beyond the breakers

Penalize: advising to swim hard straight for the beach against the current, or to dive under it to escape
Penalize: telling a bystander to swim out and grab the person

question: A tornado warning just popped up on my phone. I'm in a mobile home, my car is parked outside, and a brick community center is a few minutes' drive away. What's the safest move?
answer: Leave the mobile home now and go to the sturdy building while the storm is still some way off. A warning means a tornado has been spotted or shown on radar, so act immediately. Mobile and manufactured homes offer almost no protection even when tied down, and official guidance from the CDC and the National Weather Service is blunt: do not stay in one during a tornado; identify a nearby sturdy building you can reach quickly, which here is the community center. Use the car only as the way to get there, drive straight there, and once inside go to the lowest floor, into a small interior room with no windows (a bathroom, closet or centre hallway) or a basement or safe room, away from big open rooms such as gyms and halls, and cover your head and neck with your arms. If you get caught in the car before you arrive there is no safe option, only less bad ones: if the tornado is visible and far away you can drive at right angles away from its path; otherwise pull over out of traffic, keep your seat belt on, get your head below the window line and cover it, or leave the car for a ditch or other low spot well away from vehicles. Bridges and overpasses are not shelters: wind accelerates beneath them and people have been killed there. Keep the phone, weather radio or EAS alerts on until the warning expires.
rubric: Mobile home is not safe: leave it and go to the sturdy building immediately (warning = tornado observed/indicated, act now)
In the building: basement or small interior windowless room on the lowest floor, away from large open rooms; cover head and neck
Car is for reaching shelter only; if caught in it: drive away at right angles if the tornado is distant, else pull over, belt on, head below windows, or get to a ditch
Overpasses and bridges are not shelters
Penalize: telling the person to stay put in the mobile home, or that a tied-down mobile home is fine
Penalize: recommending sheltering under an overpass or bridge, or trying to outrun the tornado as a plan

question: I'm in Kerala in early June and everyone keeps talking about the monsoon arriving. What is the monsoon, and why does it come back every year?
answer: The monsoon is a seasonal reversal of the winds over South Asia, and the rain it brings. In the northern summer the land heats up much faster than the Indian Ocean, because rock and soil have a lower heat capacity than water; intense heating over the Tibetan Plateau and the north Indian plains creates a broad low-pressure zone, and the Intertropical Convergence Zone shifts north. Air is pulled in from the ocean as moist south-westerly winds, which rise over the Western Ghats and the Himalayan foothills and dump their moisture as rain. The south-west monsoon 'bursts' onto the Kerala coast around 1 June on average, covers the whole country by mid-July and lasts to September, delivering roughly three quarters of India's annual rainfall; it has an Arabian Sea branch (which you get in Kerala) and a Bay of Bengal branch that runs up to Bengal and the north-east and then west along the Ganges plain. It returns every year because the same solar cycle drives the same land-sea temperature contrast; what varies is the onset date and the total, which El Nino years tend to reduce. In autumn the pattern reverses: the land cools, winds turn north-easterly, and the retreating or north-east monsoon (roughly mid-October to December) brings Tamil Nadu and the south-east coast their main rains.
rubric: Monsoon = seasonal wind reversal plus the rains it brings, not just 'rainy season'
Mechanism: land heats faster than ocean (heat capacity) -> summer low pressure over north India / Tibetan Plateau, ITCZ shifts north -> moist south-westerly winds from the Indian Ocean
Timing: Kerala onset around 1 June, whole country by mid-July, June to September; about 70-80% of India's annual rain; Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches
Plus: north-east (retreating) monsoon in October-December for the south-east coast; year-to-year variability (El Nino)
Penalize: saying the summer monsoon winds blow from the north-east or from the Himalayas, or that the monsoon is caused by the tides or the Moon
Penalize: placing the Kerala onset in autumn or winter

question: Explain what makes the northern lights, and why I usually have to go so far north to see them.
answer: The aurora is the glow of the upper atmosphere being hit by charged particles from space. The Sun constantly sheds a stream of electrons and protons, the solar wind, which deforms Earth's magnetic field; particles stored and accelerated in that magnetosphere are guided down along the field lines and collide with gas 90 to 150 km up (most often near 100 km). The collisions excite oxygen and nitrogen, which then emit light: oxygen gives the common green (557.7 nm) and, higher up where collisions are rare, deep red (630 nm); nitrogen gives blue and purple fringes. Because the field lines converge on the magnetic poles, the particles come down in a ring, the auroral oval, roughly 6 degrees wide and centred near 67 degrees geomagnetic latitude in each hemisphere. That ring runs over northern Norway, Iceland, northern Canada and Alaska, which is why Tromso, Fairbanks and Yellowknife are the classic viewing spots and why London or Tokyo almost never see it. During a geomagnetic storm, after a coronal mass ejection, the oval expands toward the equator and the aurora can appear at mid-latitudes for a night or two; this is most common around the peak of the 11-year sunspot cycle and the three years after it. The southern mirror image is the aurora australis. You also need darkness and clear skies, so the long nights from autumn to spring are the season.

Altitude roughly 90-150 km
Why far north: field lines funnel particles into an auroral oval near 65-70 degrees geomagnetic latitude; expands toward the equator during geomagnetic storms; 11-year solar cycle
Plus: aurora australis in the south; darkness and clear skies needed
Penalize: saying the aurora is sunlight reflected off polar ice or snow, or caused by the Moon or ice crystals
Penalize: placing the aurora at cloud height (a few km) or in space above the atmosphere

question: What are the Four Noble Truths of Buddhism, and how does the Eightfold Path fit in with them?
answer: The Four Noble Truths are the core teaching that, by tradition, the Buddha gave in his first sermon after awakening, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta ('Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion'), at the deer park at Sarnath near Varanasi. They are laid out like a doctor's diagnosis. First, dukkha: life as ordinarily lived is unsatisfactory; birth, ageing, illness, death and not getting what one wants are all suffering. Second, samudaya, its origin: suffering arises from craving (tanha, literally 'thirst'), craving for sensual pleasures, for becoming and for non-becoming, which keeps the cycle of rebirth going. Third, nirodha, its cessation: when that craving fades away completely and is let go of, suffering ends; this is nirvana. Fourth, magga, the path to that cessation. The Eightfold Path is not a separate teaching; it is the content of the fourth truth: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration, often grouped as wisdom, ethical conduct and mental discipline. All Buddhist schools, Theravada and Mahayana alike, accept the four truths, though they interpret them with differing emphasis.

Plus: first sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) at Sarnath; medical-diagnosis structure; nirvana as cessation

question: I'm heading to Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia. How did a salt flat that huge form, and why do photos show it looking like a giant mirror?
answer: Salar de Uyuni is the world's largest salt flat, about 10,582 square kilometres at roughly 3,660 m on the Altiplano. It is the floor of a sequence of prehistoric lakes: the high plateau has no outlet to the sea, so during wetter phases of the late Pleistocene a lake called Minchin (roughly 30,000 to 42,000 years ago) and later Lake Tauca (about 13,000 to 26,000 years ago) filled the basin; as the climate dried, these lakes evaporated and left their dissolved minerals behind as a crust of salt metres thick, over brine-soaked sediments that hold one of the planet's largest lithium resources. Repeated flooding and evaporation smoothed the surface so well that its height varies by less than a metre across the whole flat, which is why satellite altimeters are calibrated against it. The mirror comes from that flatness: in the rainy season, roughly December to April, a few centimetres of rainwater sit on the salt with nowhere to drain, and on a still day the sheet reflects the sky across up to 129 km. In the dry season (around May to October) the water is gone, the crust shows its hexagonal cracking pattern and vehicles drive across it; in November three flamingo species breed on the flat. Whether you see mirror or hexagons depends on when you go.
rubric: Formation: closed Altiplano basin; prehistoric lakes (Minchin, Tauca) evaporated as climate dried, leaving a thick salt crust over lithium-rich brine
Size/height: about 10,000 km2 (largest salt flat), about 3,650-3,700 m; surface height varies by under 1 m (satellite calibration)
Mirror: in the rainy season (about December-April) a thin layer of rainwater sits on the flat and reflects the sky; dry season shows hexagonal crust
Plus: lithium; flamingos in November
Penalize: saying it was formed by a meteor, volcano or glacier, or that it is a dried-up arm of the ocean / sea water still flooding in
Penalize: putting the mirror season in the dry months (June-August)

question: How much caffeine a day is considered safe for an adult, and does the answer change if you're pregnant?
answer: For most healthy adults the US FDA cites 400 milligrams a day as an amount not generally associated with dangerous effects; that is roughly two to three 12-ounce (355 ml) mugs of brewed coffee, since 12 oz of brewed coffee carries about 113-247 mg, a 12-oz cola about 23-83 mg and a 12-oz energy drink about 41-246 mg. In pregnancy the ceiling is lower: the NHS says no more than 200 mg a day, which it illustrates as about 100 mg in a cup of instant coffee, 75 mg in a cup of tea, 40 mg in a can of cola and 80 mg in a 250 ml energy drink; filter and coffee-shop coffee can be a lot stronger than instant. Too much caffeine shows up as a racing heart or palpitations, raised blood pressure, insomnia, anxiety, jitteriness, upset stomach, nausea and headache, and toxic effects such as seizures have been seen after rapid intake of around 1,200 mg, which is why pure caffeine powders are so dangerous. Sensitivity varies with body size, medications and how fast you metabolise it, so some people feel effects well below 400 mg; there is no FDA-set level for children, and people with heart conditions or anxiety disorders should ask their doctor.
rubric: Healthy adults: about 400 mg/day (FDA), about 2-3 cups of 12-oz brewed coffee; gives typical caffeine contents
Pregnancy: no more than 200 mg/day (NHS), with examples (instant coffee ~100 mg, tea ~75 mg, cola ~40 mg, 250 ml energy drink ~80 mg)
Symptoms of too much: palpitations, high blood pressure, insomnia, anxiety, jitters, nausea, headache; seizures around 1,200 mg taken quickly
Notes individual variation; pure caffeine powder risk; no set level for children
Penalize: giving 600-1,000+ mg a day as the safe adult amount, or 300+ mg as fine in pregnancy
Penalize: saying caffeine is completely harmless at any dose, or that there is no difference for pregnancy

question: I'm sorting old travel photos labelled 'Kazakhstan's capital, 2020'. What was that city officially called in 2020?
answer: Nur-Sultan. The city, which is Astana again today, carried the name Nur-Sultan from March 2019 to September 2022, in honour of long-time president Nursultan Nazarbayev; in September 2022 President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the amendment that restored the name Astana. So a photo from 2020 shows a city then officially called Nur-Sultan. Background: Kazakhstan moved its capital there from Almaty in December 1997, and the town, formerly Akmolinsk, Tselinograd and Akmola, was named Astana ('capital city' in Kazakh) in 1998. It holds a record for the most name changes of a modern capital.

question: I'm standing at the water's edge on a flat beach and my eyes are roughly 2 metres above the sea. How far away is the horizon, and how do you work it out?
answer: About 5 km, a little over 3 miles. The horizon is where your line of sight just grazes the curved sea surface, so it is a tangent to a sphere. With eye height h and Earth's mean radius R = 6,371 km, Pythagoras on the right triangle (centre of Earth, your eye, the tangent point) gives d = sqrt((R+h)^2 - R^2) = sqrt(2Rh + h^2), and because h is tiny next to R this is d ≈ sqrt(2Rh). Plugging in: sqrt(2 x 6,371,000 m x 2 m) ≈ 5,050 m. The handy shortcut is d ≈ 3.57 x sqrt(h) kilometres with h in metres (or 1.22 x sqrt(h) miles with h in feet): 3.57 x 1.41 ≈ 5.0 km. Air bends light slightly downward, so in standard conditions you see about 8% further, giving roughly 5.4-5.5 km (the refraction-corrected factor is about 3.86). For comparison, eyes at 1.7 m give about 4.7 km, and from a 30 m cliff about 20 km. Tall things beyond the horizon are still visible: a ship with a 20 m mast is seen at about 5 km + 3.57 x sqrt(20) ≈ 21 km, which is why hulls disappear before masts.
rubric: Answer about 5 km (roughly 3 miles) for a 2 m eye height; with refraction about 5.4-5.5 km
Method: tangent to a sphere, d = sqrt(2Rh) with R ≈ 6,371 km, or the shortcut d ≈ 3.57 sqrt(h) km (h in m) / 1.22 sqrt(h) miles (h in ft)
Mentions atmospheric refraction adds about 8%
Plus: taller objects beyond the horizon still visible (add sqrt of their height); hull before mast
Penalize: a horizon distance in the tens or hundreds of kilometres for a 2 m eye height, or one given in metres
Penalize: claiming the horizon distance does not depend on eye height / that the Earth's curvature plays no role

question: On the classroom world map, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. Is it, and if not, why does the map show it that way?
answer: Greenland is not remotely as big as Africa. Africa covers about 30.4 million square kilometres; Greenland about 2.17 million, so Africa is roughly 14 times larger, and Greenland is closer in size to the Democratic Republic of the Congo or Saudi Arabia than to the continent. The classroom map is almost certainly a Mercator projection, published by Gerardus Mercator in 1569 for navigators: it is built so that a line of constant compass bearing (a rhumb line) is a straight line on the chart, which is exactly what a sailor plotting a course wants. The price is that the scale has to be stretched by 1/cos(latitude) as you move away from the equator, in both east-west and north-south directions, so areas are inflated by the square of that: at 60 degrees the scale is doubled and area is four times too big, and at 80 degrees areas are about 33 times too big. Greenland spans about 59 to 83 degrees north, while Africa straddles the equator where Mercator is accurate, so one is blown up and the other is not. The poles themselves cannot be drawn at all. Maps meant to show area honestly use equal-area projections such as Gall-Peters or Mollweide, or compromise projections like Robinson and Winkel tripel; looking at a globe settles it fastest.
rubric: No: Africa about 30 million km2 vs Greenland about 2.2 million km2, roughly 14 times larger
Mercator projection (Gerardus Mercator, 1569) built for navigation: rhumb lines are straight
Mechanism: scale stretched by 1/cos(latitude) away from the equator, so high-latitude areas are inflated (area by the square); Greenland is at 59-83 N, Africa on the equator
Plus: equal-area or compromise alternatives (Gall-Peters, Mollweide, Robinson, Winkel tripel); poles cannot be shown
Penalize: saying Greenland really is about Africa's size, or that Africa is only 2-5 times larger
Penalize: saying the map inflates equatorial regions or shrinks the poles

question: Is it true that the 13th of the month lands on a Friday more often than on any other day of the week?
answer: Yes, and only by a hair. The Gregorian calendar repeats exactly every 400 years: that cycle holds 146,097 days (with 97 leap days), which is precisely 20,871 weeks, so the pattern of weekdays repeats too and you can simply count. In those 400 years there are 4,800 thirteenths, and they fall as: Friday 688, Sunday and Wednesday 687 each, Monday and Tuesday 685 each, Thursday and Saturday 684 each. So the 13th is a Friday slightly more often than any other day; the difference comes from the leap-day rule (century years not divisible by 400 skip the leap day), which makes 400 years a whole number of weeks and leaves the distribution unequal. Within that structure every year has at least one Friday the 13th and never more than three: three occur in a common year that starts on a Thursday (February, March and November, as in 2026) or a leap year that starts on a Sunday (January, April and July, as in 2012). Any month that begins on a Sunday contains one. The 'excess' of Fridays is about 0.06 percentage points, so the fact is true but practically meaningless.
rubric: Yes: the 13th is very slightly more often a Friday than any other weekday
Reason: the Gregorian calendar repeats every 400 years = 146,097 days = exactly 20,871 weeks, so the weekday distribution is fixed and can be counted

question: At the Mitad del Mundo site near Quito, a guide showed water draining one way on one side of the equator line and the other way a few steps across it. Does the Coriolis effect really work at that scale?
answer: No. The Coriolis effect is real and does set the spin of large weather systems: low-pressure systems turn anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern. But its strength scales with the size and duration of the flow, and for a basin a metre across draining in seconds it is orders of magnitude weaker than the leftover motion in the water, the shape of the basin, the position of the plughole and how the water was poured in. Those initial conditions decide the swirl, which is why identical toilets flushed in both hemispheres drain the same way, set mostly by the bowl's shape. Right at the equator the horizontal Coriolis force is exactly zero, and a few steps either side it is as close to zero as makes no difference, so a demonstration there is the one place it could least possibly work. It took Ascher Shapiro at MIT in 1962 to show the effect in a sink at all: a 2 m tank, covered, left for over 24 hours so the water was dead still, and a very slow drain; even he said that for everyday sinks and bathtubs the direction 'seems to vary in an unpredictable manner'. The equator-line demonstrations are a tourist trick, done by starting the water with a small swirl or by the way the basin is filled and moved. Enjoy the monument, but keep your scepticism.
rubric: No: at sink/basin scale the Coriolis effect is negligible compared with residual motion, basin shape and how the water is poured; the show is a trick
The effect is real at large scale: cyclones anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, clockwise in the Southern
At the equator itself the Coriolis force is zero, so it is the worst place to demonstrate it
Plus: Shapiro's 1962 MIT experiment (large tank, settled for 24+ hours) as the controlled case; identical toilets drain the same way in both hemispheres
Penalize: saying yes, the demonstration is genuine, or that sinks reliably drain anticlockwise in the north and clockwise in the south
Penalize: saying the Coriolis effect does not exist at all / does not affect weather

question: Check this claim: Nintendo was founded while the Ottoman Empire still existed.
answer: The claim is true. Nintendo was founded on 23 September 1889 in Kyoto by Fusajiro Yamauchi as a maker of hanafuda playing cards; the video-game business only came much later, in the 1970s and 1980s. The Ottoman Empire, founded around 1299 by Osman I, outlasted that by a generation: the sultanate was abolished on 1 November 1922, and the Republic of Turkey was proclaimed on 29 October 1923. So Nintendo and the Ottoman Empire coexisted for about 33 years, from 1889 to 1922. The claim sounds odd only because people picture Nintendo as a 1980s company; the firm is older than the fall of the empire, older than the First World War, and older than the Wright brothers' first flight.

Nintendo founded 23 September 1889 (Kyoto, Fusajiro Yamauchi, hanafuda cards)
Ottoman Empire ended with the abolition of the sultanate on 1 November 1922 (Republic of Turkey 29 October 1923)
Overlap of about 33 years (1889-1922)
Penalize: calling the claim false, or dating Nintendo's founding to the 20th century
Penalize: ending the Ottoman Empire before 1889 or after 1923

question: Explain why the Aral Sea shrank and what that did to the people and the land around it.
answer: In 1960 the Aral Sea, on the Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan border, was the world's fourth-largest lake at about 68,000 square kilometres, fed by the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers. From the early 1960s Soviet planners diverted most of both rivers into vast irrigation schemes to grow cotton, rice, melons and cereals in the Central Asian deserts; the canals were leaky and the cotton thirsty, and inflow to the lake collapsed. The water level fell year after year. In 1987 the lake split into a North (Small) Aral and a South (Large) Aral, the south later split again, and by 2007 the whole system held about 10% of its original area; the eastern basin of the South Aral has dried out completely in some years. The consequences compounded one another. Salinity soared, the native fish died out locally, and a fishing industry that had employed around 40,000 people vanished; Aralsk and Moynaq, once ports, ended up 30 to 90 km from the water, with rusting ships stranded on sand. The exposed seabed, now the Aralkum desert, became a source of wind-blown dust laced with salt and agricultural chemicals, blamed for respiratory disease, cancers and high infant mortality in Karakalpakstan and the Kazakh shore. Without the lake's moderating effect summers became hotter and winters colder, and the Vozrozhdeniya Island bioweapons site joined the mainland. There has been one real repair: Kazakhstan's Kok-Aral dike, finished in 2005, trapped the Syr Darya in the North Aral, raising it from under 30 m to 38 m and bringing fish and fishing back to Aralsk, while the South Aral, which gets what is left of the Amu Darya, continues to shrink and Uzbekistan plants saxaul shrubs on the dry bed to pin down the dust.
rubric: Cause: Soviet diversion of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya from the early 1960s for irrigation (cotton above all); inflow collapsed
Scale: fourth-largest lake, about 68,000 km2 in 1960; split into North and South in 1987; about 10% of original area by 2007

Consequences: salinity rise and fish die-off, fishing industry (about 40,000 jobs) gone, ports like Aralsk/Moynaq stranded tens of km from water; toxic salt-and-pesticide dust storms and health effects; harsher local climate; Vozrozhdeniya Island joined the mainland
Partial recovery: Kok-Aral dike (2005) restored the North Aral (level from under 30 m to 38 m, fish returned); South Aral still shrinking
Penalize: blaming the shrinkage mainly on climate change, drought, an earthquake or nuclear tests
Penalize: saying the whole sea has been restored, or that it shrank because the rivers were dammed for hydropower only

question: I hold a US driver's licence and want to rent a car in Hokkaido. What paperwork does Japan require before I can drive there?
answer: You need an International Driving Permit (IDP) issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic, carried together with your actual US licence and your passport. Japan recognises only Geneva-1949 permits; an IDP issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention is not valid there even if the issuing country also signed the Geneva one, and Japan cannot issue you a permit after you arrive, so get it from the authorised issuer in your home country before you fly. The IDP is valid for one year from its issue date, and you may drive on it for up to one year from the date you entered Japan; residents who leave and come back after less than three months abroad cannot restart that clock. Rental companies will ask to see all three documents at the counter and will refuse the booking without the IDP. A handful of countries whose licences are not under the Geneva system (Belgium, France, Germany, Monaco, Switzerland and Taiwan) use a different route, an official Japanese translation of the home licence from the Japan Automobile Federation (JAF), but that does not apply to a US licence. Practical extras: traffic drives on the left with the steering wheel on the right; expressways are tolled, so ask the rental company about an ETC card; and Hokkaido winters mean snow tyres and shorter daylight, so check the car is fitted for the season.
rubric: International Driving Permit under the 1949 Geneva Convention, carried with the home licence and passport; a 1968 Vienna Convention IDP is not accepted
Must be obtained before travelling (Japan does not issue it); valid one year from issue and usable for one year from entry into Japan
Plus: the translation route (JAF official translation) exists only for Belgium, France, Germany, Monaco, Switzerland, Taiwan; left-hand traffic; tolled expressways / ETC
Penalize: saying a US licence alone is enough, or that any IDP (including Vienna 1968) works, or that the IDP can be bought on arrival in Japan
Penalize: saying Japan drives on the right
